decks.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity — Part 1: Development of the table, blocks and positions
goals: Trace the development of the periodic table from triads to the modern periodic law
Name and write symbols for elements with atomic number above 100
Classify elements into s, p, d and f blocks and find period and group from the configuration
Distinguish metals, non-metals, metalloids, representative, transition and inner transition elements

slides.heading: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a hundred and eighteen elements came to be arranged in one table, and how to read an element’s position from its electrons.

visual.alt: Table of four stages in the development of the periodic table and the basis used in each

slides.narration: Why do we need a periodic table at all? Because over a hundred elements are far too many to study one by one. Chemists spent about a century finding the right way to sort them. In this part we follow that story, learn how new elements are named, and then learn to read an element’s block, period and group from its electron arrangement.

slides.heading: Döbereiner’s triads
slides.body_md: In 1817 Döbereiner noticed groups of **three elements** with similar properties in which the **atomic mass of the middle element is close to the average** of the other two.

visual.alt: Table of three Döbereiner triads with the atomic masses and the average of the outer two

slides.narration: Döbereiner found families of three. In the lithium, sodium, potassium family, the average of the outer two masses is exactly the mass of sodium. For calcium, strontium and barium, and for chlorine, bromine and iodine, the average is close to the middle element. The idea was sound but only a handful of triads could be found.

slides.heading: Newlands’ law of octaves
slides.body_md: In 1866 Newlands arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found that **every eighth element resembled the first**, like notes in a musical octave. It worked only up to **calcium**; the noble gases were still unknown.

visual.alt: Table of the first two Newlands octaves showing that sodium resembles lithium and chlorine resembles fluorine

slides.narration: Newlands listed the elements by mass and noticed that sodium behaves like lithium, magnesium like beryllium, and chlorine like fluorine: every eighth element repeated the pattern. This was the first clear statement of periodicity. But it broke down after calcium, and it left no room for elements still to be discovered, so chemists did not accept it.

slides.heading: Mendeleev’s periodic law
slides.body_md: **Law (1869):** the properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic masses**. Mendeleev arranged elements in rows and columns so that similar ones fell in the same group, and he **left gaps** for elements not yet discovered.

rows: Iodine placed after tellurium by properties, although lighter
Used hydride and oxide formulae to place elements

visual.alt: Table of four features of Mendeleev’s periodic table

slides.narration: Mendeleev went further than Newlands. He was prepared to break the order of mass when properties demanded it, as with tellurium and iodine, and he boldly left gaps for elements that had not yet been found. He also checked the formulae of the hydrides and oxides of each element, so that members of a group formed similar compounds.

slides.heading: Mendeleev’s predictions and limitations
slides.body_md: He named the missing elements **eka-boron**, **eka-aluminium** and **eka-silicon** and predicted their properties. The later discoveries matched closely, which won acceptance for the table. Limitations: **hydrogen** has no clear place, **isotopes** have no place, and some pairs are in the wrong mass order.

visual.alt: Table comparing the atomic masses Mendeleev predicted for three missing elements with the elements later found

slides.narration: The great success of the table was prediction. Mendeleev described eka-aluminium and eka-silicon in detail, and when gallium and germanium were found, their masses and properties matched. The weaknesses were also clear: hydrogen fitted nowhere well, isotopes of one element would need different places, and a few pairs were in the wrong order of mass.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the triad rule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Döbereiner’s rule says the middle mass is the average of the outer two. Use it for sulfur (32.1), selenium and tellurium (127.6), given that selenium has mass 79.0 by experiment. How close is the rule?

**Step 1.** Average of the outer two: $\dfrac{32.1 + 127.6}{2} = 79.85$.

**Step 2.** Difference from the observed value: $79.85 - 79.0 = 0.85$.

**Conclusion.** The rule works to within about one unit, so S, Se, Te form a good triad.

nodes.label: A small difference means a triad

visual.alt: Flow for testing a triad: average the outer masses and compare with the middle element

slides.narration: To test a triad, add the masses of the outer two elements and halve the result. For sulfur and tellurium the average comes out just under eighty, against an experimental value of seventy nine for selenium. A difference of less than one unit is small, so the three elements do form a triad in the sense of Döbereiner.

slides.heading: The modern periodic law
slides.body_md: In 1913 **Moseley** showed from X-ray spectra that the **nuclear charge (atomic number)**, not mass, is the true basis. **Modern law:** the properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic numbers**. This removes Mendeleev’s mass-order anomalies.

visual.alt: Table of three element pairs whose order by atomic mass is reversed but whose order by atomic number is correct

slides.narration: Moseley measured X-ray frequencies and found that they depend on the nuclear charge, that is, the atomic number. When elements are ordered by atomic number, argon comes before potassium, cobalt before nickel, and tellurium before iodine, exactly as their chemistry demands. So the modern law uses atomic number, and the old anomalies disappear.

slides.heading: The long form: periods and groups
slides.body_md: The long form has **18 groups** (columns) and **7 periods** (rows). Each period begins when a new shell starts filling, so **period length = electrons that fill that stretch of subshells**.

visual.alt: Table of the seven periods with the subshells that fill in each and the number of elements; the total is one hundred and eighteen

slides.narration: The first period has only two elements, because only the first s subshell fills. The second and third periods fill s and p, giving eight each. The fourth and fifth add the ten d electrons, giving eighteen. The sixth and seventh also add fourteen f electrons, giving thirty two. All together that makes one hundred and eighteen elements.

slides.heading: Naming elements with Z greater than 100
slides.body_md: Until an element is confirmed, IUPAC gives a **temporary systematic name** built from numerical roots, one per digit of the atomic number, ending in **-ium**. The **symbol** is the first letters of the roots, three letters in all.

visual.alt: Table of the numerical roots for digits zero to nine used in systematic element names

slides.narration: For a new element, IUPAC writes the atomic number digit by digit as roots: nil for zero, un for one, bi for two, tri for three, and so on up to enn for nine. Join the roots and add the ending ium. The symbol takes the first letter of each root, with a capital for the first. Elements up to one hundred and eighteen now have permanent names.

slides.heading: Worked example: systematic names
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the systematic name and symbol of the element with (a) $Z = 119$, (b) $Z = 123$, and the atomic number of (c) unquadnilium.

**(a)** 1 → un, 1 → un, 9 → enn: **ununennium**, symbol **Uue**.

**(b)** 1 → un, 2 → bi, 3 → tri: **unbitrium** (the final i of tri is not doubled), symbol **Ubt**.

**(c)** un = 1, quad = 4, nil = 0: $Z = 140$.

visual.alt: Table of three atomic numbers above one hundred with their roots, systematic names and symbols

slides.narration: Take each digit in turn. For atomic number one hundred and nineteen the digits are one, one and nine, which give un, un and enn, so the name is ununennium. For one hundred and twenty three we get un, bi, tri and add ium. Going backwards, unquadnilium has the digits one, four and zero, so its atomic number is one hundred and forty.

slides.heading: Classifying by the last subshell: s, p, d and f blocks
slides.body_md: The **block** is the subshell that receives the **last electron** (Aufbau order): **s** (groups 1–2 and He), **p** (groups 13–18), **d** (groups 3–12) and **f** (lanthanoids and actinoids, placed below).

visual.caption: Schematic only: each small box is one element.

slides.narration: Look at the picture, which is only a schematic of the table. The first two groups form the s block, along with helium. On the right, six groups make the p block. In the middle, ten groups form the d block, which starts in the fourth period. Below the table sit the f block elements, fourteen lanthanoids and fourteen actinoids.

slides.heading: Finding period and group from the configuration
slides.body_md: **Period** = principal quantum number of the **outermost shell**. **Group:** s-block = number of valence electrons; p-block = 12 + number of p electrons; d-block = (n−1)d electrons + ns electrons (groups 3–12).

visual.alt: Table of the general valence configuration and group number range for the s, p, d and f blocks

slides.narration: The period is simply the highest shell number that holds electrons. For the group, count differently in each block. In the s block, the group is the number of valence electrons. In the p block, add twelve to the number of p electrons. In the d block, add the d electrons and the s electrons, which gives groups three to twelve.

slides.heading: Worked example: locating elements
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the block, period and group of the elements with $Z = 33$, $Z = 48$ and $Z = 56$.

**Z = 33:** [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³ → last electron in 4p (3 electrons): **p-block, period 4, group 15**.

**Z = 48:** [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² → last electron in 4d: **d-block, period 5, group 12** (10 + 2).

**Z = 56:** [Xe] 6s² → **s-block, period 6, group 2**.

visual.alt: Table of the configuration, block, period and group of the elements with atomic numbers thirty three, forty eight and fifty six

slides.narration: Write the configuration, then read off the answer. Atomic number thirty three ends in three p electrons in the fourth shell, so it is a p block element in period four and group fifteen. Forty eight ends with a full d subshell and two s electrons, giving the d block, period five, group twelve. Fifty six ends in six s two: s block, period six, group two.

slides.heading: Quick check: block and group
slides.body_md: Locate an element from its valence configuration.
slides.narration: Quick check. Find the last subshell to fill, and count electrons as the rule for that block says.

slides.heading: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
slides.body_md: About **four-fifths** of the elements are **metals**: lustrous, malleable, good conductors, usually forming cations. **Non-metals** (at the top right) form anions or share electrons. **Metalloids** along the staircase line are in between: **B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te**.

rows: Gain or share electrons; acidic oxides
B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te

visual.alt: Table comparing metals, non-metals and metalloids with examples and behaviour

slides.narration: Most elements are metals. They conduct heat and electricity, can be hammered into sheets, and tend to lose electrons to form positive ions. Non-metals are found at the top right of the table and gain or share electrons. Between them, along a staircase line, sit the metalloids, such as silicon and germanium, which are semiconductors.

slides.heading: Representative, transition and inner transition elements
slides.body_md: The **s- and p-block** elements (except group 18) are **representative** or main group elements. The **d-block** are **transition elements**; the **f-block** are **inner transition elements**. **Noble gases** (group 18) have filled shells: ns² np⁶ (He: 1s²).

visual.alt: Table of representative, transition, inner transition and noble gas categories with their blocks and defining feature

slides.narration: Another way to sort elements is by what is filling. In representative elements the outer shell is filling. In transition elements an inner d subshell fills. In inner transition elements an f subshell two shells in fills. And noble gases have complete outer shells, which explains why they are so unreactive.

slides.body_md: Identify the metalloid or the category from a property or position.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the staircase line, and which blocks are called transition and inner transition.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Döbereiner (triads), Newlands (octaves), Mendeleev (periodic law by mass, gaps, predictions) led to Moseley’s modern law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
Long form: 18 groups, 7 periods; period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 (118 elements).
Z > 100: digit roots nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn + ium; symbol = first letters.
Block = subshell of the last electron; period = outer shell number; group rules differ by block.
Metals, non-metals, metalloids; representative, transition, inner transition; noble gases.

visual.alt: Summary table of the four blocks, the subshell receiving the last electron and the groups

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Classification moved from triads and octaves to Mendeleev’s law, and then to the modern law based on atomic number. The long form table has eighteen groups and seven periods. New elements get systematic names from digit roots. An element’s block comes from its last electron, and its period and group follow from the outer shells.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: State the modern law with the words “atomic number”, not “atomic mass”.
Give two reasons when asked why Mendeleev’s table was accepted: predictions and gaps.
For Z > 100 names, write roots digit by digit, then add “ium”.
Write the full configuration before deciding block, period and group.
Remember helium is s-block but sits in group 18.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. In the modern periodic law, always say atomic number. When describing Mendeleev, mention gaps and successful predictions. For element names, work digit by digit. For group numbers of d block elements, add the d and s electrons together. And do not forget that helium is an s block element placed with the noble gases.

slides.heading: Periodic trends
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why atomic size, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity change in regular ways across periods and down groups.

visual.alt: Table of the general trends of four properties across a period and down a group

slides.narration: Because electron arrangements repeat, properties repeat too. Moving across a period, nuclear charge rises while the shell number stays the same, so atoms shrink and hold their electrons more tightly. Moving down a group, new shells are added, so atoms grow and let go of electrons more easily. This part explains each property and its exceptions.

slides.heading: Atomic radius
slides.body_md: **Covalent radius** is half the distance between two bonded atoms of one element; **metallic radius** is half the distance between neighbouring metal ions; **van der Waals radius** is for non-bonded atoms and is always larger. Across a period, **nuclear charge rises** with no new shell, so the radius **falls**; down a group, a **new shell** is added, so it **rises**.

visual.alt: Table of atomic radii in picometres (metallic radii for the metals, covalent radii for the non-metals) of the elements of the second and third periods, decreasing from left to right

slides.narration: The size of an atom cannot be measured directly, so we use half the bond length. In a period, each element has one more proton but electrons enter the same shell, so the pull increases and the atom shrinks. In a group, each step down adds a whole shell and the atom grows. Van der Waals radii are always larger than covalent radii.

slides.heading: Ionic radius
slides.body_md: A **cation** is smaller than its atom (electrons lost, or a whole shell lost, and the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons). An **anion** is larger (more electrons repel each other against the same nuclear charge). More positive charge means smaller: $\ce{Fe^3+}$ < $\ce{Fe^2+}$.

visual.alt: Table comparing atom and ion radii showing that cations are smaller and anions larger than their atoms

slides.narration: Compare each atom with its ion. Sodium loses its outer shell, so the sodium ion is much smaller. Chlorine gains an electron without a new proton, so repulsion between electrons swells the ion and the chloride ion is far larger than the atom. The more positive charge an ion carries, the harder the nucleus pulls on the remaining electrons, so the smaller it is.

slides.heading: Isoelectronic species
slides.body_md: **Isoelectronic** species have the **same number of electrons**. The one with the **higher nuclear charge** is smaller. Here every ion has ten electrons, so the radius falls from N³⁻ to Al³⁺.

Aluminium has thirteen protons for the same ten electrons, so it is the smallest. Same electrons, rising nuclear charge, shrinking size.

slides.heading: Worked example: arranging by radius
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in increasing order of radius: (a) $\ce{K+}$, $\ce{Ca^2+}$, $\ce{Cl-}$, $\ce{S^2-}$; (b) Fe, $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$.

**(a)** All have 18 electrons (isoelectronic with Ar). Nuclear charges: Ca 20 > K 19 > Cl 17 > S 16. Higher charge, smaller size: $\ce{Ca^2+}$ < $\ce{K+}$ < $\ce{Cl-}$ < $\ce{S^2-}$ (100, 138, 181 and 184 pm).

**(b)** Same nucleus; fewer electrons gives a smaller ion: $\ce{Fe^3+}$ < $\ce{Fe^2+}$ < Fe.

visual.alt: Table of four ions with eighteen electrons, their nuclear charges and radii in picometres

slides.narration: First check that the species are isoelectronic. Calcium, potassium, chloride and sulfide ions all have eighteen electrons, so the order follows nuclear charge: calcium ion smallest and sulfide largest. For the iron series the nucleus is the same, so the more electrons removed, the more the rest are pulled in: the iron three plus ion is the smallest.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: The **ionisation enthalpy** is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It rises with **nuclear charge** and falls with **larger size** and **screening** by inner electrons. For a given shell, penetration makes it **s > p > d > f**.

rows: Penetration of the orbital (s > p > d > f)

visual.alt: Table of five factors and their effect on ionisation enthalpy

slides.narration: Ionisation enthalpy is the price of taking one electron from a gaseous atom. It is higher when the nucleus pulls harder, so more nuclear charge raises it. It is lower when the electron is far away or shielded by inner electrons. And an electron in an orbital that penetrates close to the nucleus, such as an s orbital, is held more tightly than one in a p orbital.

slides.heading: Trend in first ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: Across each period the value **generally rises** to a peak at the noble gas, then falls sharply at the alkali metal of the next period. Down a group it **falls**.

slides.narration: Here is the graph for the first twenty elements. Each period climbs from the alkali metal to the noble gas, and then drops sharply to the next alkali metal, which has a new shell. Notice that the climb is not smooth: there are small dips at boron, oxygen, aluminium and sulfur. Those are the anomalies we explain next.

slides.heading: Anomalies in ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: **Be > B:** the 2s electron of Be is more penetrating than the 2p electron of B. **N > O:** N has a stable half-filled 2p³; in O two electrons share an orbital and repel, so one is easier to remove. The same applies to **Mg > Al** and **P > S**.

visual.alt: Table of four pairs of neighbouring elements with the first ionisation enthalpies showing the anomalies

slides.narration: Why does boron have lower ionisation enthalpy than beryllium, even though it has more protons? Its outermost electron is in a p orbital, which is shielded by the filled s subshell, so it is easier to remove. And why is nitrogen higher than oxygen? Nitrogen has a stable half filled p subshell, while in oxygen paired electrons repel each other, so one leaves more easily.

slides.heading: Successive ionisation enthalpies
slides.body_md: Each removal is harder than the last because the **same nuclear charge** holds **fewer electrons**. A very large **jump** appears when electrons are removed from an inner, filled shell: this shows the number of **valence electrons**.

visual.alt: Table of successive ionisation enthalpies in kilojoules per mole of sodium, magnesium and aluminium with a large jump after the valence electrons are removed

slides.narration: Look at the jumps. For sodium, the second value is almost ten times the first, because the second electron must come from a filled inner shell. For magnesium, the big jump comes after two electrons, and for aluminium after three. So the position of the jump tells us how many valence electrons an element has, and hence its group.

slides.heading: Worked example: group from successive data
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An element X has successive ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): 786, 1577, 3232, 4356, 16091. Find its group and the formula of its chloride.

**Step 1.** Ratios of successive values: 2.0, 2.0, 1.3, 3.7.

**Step 2.** The largest jump (3.7×) follows the **fourth** value, so X has **4 valence electrons**: group 14 (p-block).

**Step 3.** Valency 4, so the chloride is $\ce{XCl4}$.

visual.alt: Table of the five successive ionisation enthalpies with ratios showing the largest jump after the fourth

slides.narration: Work out the ratio of each value to the one before it. The ratios are two, two, one point three, and then three point seven. The big jump comes when the fifth electron is removed, which means the first four were valence electrons. Four valence electrons put the element in group fourteen, and a chloride with formula X C l four.

slides.heading: Electron gain enthalpy
slides.body_md: The **electron gain enthalpy** is the enthalpy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron. A **negative** value means energy is released. It is **most negative for halogens**; noble gases have **positive** values (the electron must enter a new shell). Adding a second electron (O⁻ → O²⁻) is always **endothermic** because of repulsion.

visual.alt: Table of electron gain enthalpies of fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, oxygen and sulfur

slides.narration: Electron gain enthalpy tells how willing an atom is to accept an electron. The more negative the value, the more energy is released. Halogens release the most, because one extra electron completes their outer shell. Noble gases have positive values, because the new electron would have to start a new shell. The second electron added to an ion is always resisted.

slides.heading: Why chlorine releases more energy than fluorine
slides.body_md: Fluorine is so small that its 2p subshell is **crowded**: the incoming electron is repelled by the electrons already there. Chlorine’s larger 3p subshell has more room, so chlorine has the **more negative** value. The same pattern appears for O and S.

slides.narration: You might expect fluorine to be best at gaining electrons, but the data say chlorine is better. Fluorine’s atom is so small that its second shell is crowded, so the incoming electron feels strong repulsion. Chlorine has more space. Oxygen and sulfur show the same effect, which is why sulfur has the larger bar.

slides.heading: Electronegativity
slides.body_md: **Electronegativity** is the tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons in a bond. On the **Pauling scale** F = 4.0 is highest. It **increases across a period** and **decreases down a group**; it is greater for elements that readily form anions.

visual.alt: Table of Pauling electronegativity values of the second-period and third-period elements

slides.narration: Electronegativity describes an atom inside a bond, not an isolated atom. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and the value rises across a period as atoms get smaller. It falls down a group. A large difference in electronegativity between two atoms means a polar or even ionic bond. Notice that lithium and magnesium, or beryllium and aluminium, have nearly equal values.

slides.heading: Valency and chemical character across a period
slides.body_md: **Valency** is the number of H or Cl atoms (or twice the number of O atoms) an atom combines with: 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1 across period 3 for the hydrides; for oxides it rises from 1 to 7. Oxides change from **basic** (Na₂O, MgO) to **amphoteric** (Al₂O₃) to **acidic** (SiO₂ to Cl₂O₇).

visual.alt: Table of the oxides, their acid-base nature and the hydrides of the third-period elements

slides.narration: Valency can be read from formulae. Across period three the hydride valency goes one, two, three, four, then back down to three, two, one, because non-metals combine with hydrogen to complete an octet. Oxides change character in an equally orderly way: sodium and magnesium oxides are basic, aluminium oxide is amphoteric, and the rest are acidic.

slides.heading: Worked example: an amphoteric oxide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.

It reacts with an **acid** as a base: $\ce{Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O}$.

It reacts with a **base** as an acid: $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O -> 2NaAl(OH)4}$.

Because it reacts with both, it is **amphoteric**. Its position between basic MgO and acidic SiO₂ across the period is no accident.

visual.alt: Table of how basic, amphoteric and acidic oxides react with acids and bases

slides.narration: An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases. Aluminium oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid, acting as a base, and also in sodium hydroxide, acting as an acid. Oxides on its left only react with acids; oxides on its right only react with bases. Aluminium sits exactly at the changeover.

slides.heading: Anomalous behaviour of second-period elements
slides.body_md: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F differ from the rest of their groups because of **small size**, **high electronegativity** and ionisation enthalpy, and **no d orbitals**, so the maximum covalence is **4**. They also form pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, N≡N, O=O).

rows: No d orbitals, covalence limited to 4

visual.alt: Table of three differences between second-period elements and the next member of the group

slides.narration: The first element of each group is unusual. Its atom is small, strongly electronegative, and has no d orbitals, so it cannot have more than four bonds. Nitrogen forms only the trichloride, while phosphorus forms a pentachloride too. Small atoms also form strong double and triple bonds with themselves, as in nitrogen gas and oxygen gas, which their heavier relatives do not.

slides.heading: Diagonal relationships
slides.body_md: Elements in a period and the next one in the **next group diagonally** resemble each other: **Li–Mg**, **Be–Al**, **B–Si**. The reason is a similar **charge-to-size ratio** and electronegativity.

rows: Both form nitrides directly; both carbonates decompose on heating; both form covalent chlorides soluble in ethanol
Both oxides are amphoteric; both have the same electronegativity (1.5); both chlorides are covalent
Both are metalloids; both oxides are acidic; both form volatile hydrides

visual.alt: Table of three diagonal pairs with the properties they share

slides.narration: Moving one step to the right makes the charge higher, and moving one step down makes the size larger. These two changes cancel, so the diagonal neighbour has a similar charge to size ratio. That is why lithium resembles magnesium, beryllium resembles aluminium, and boron resembles silicon, both in physical properties and in the behaviour of their compounds.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Atomic radius: decreases across a period, increases down a group; cations smaller, anions larger; among isoelectronic ions, higher nuclear charge means smaller.
Ionisation enthalpy: rises across a period (exceptions Be/B, N/O, Mg/Al, P/S), falls down a group; successive values jump after valence electrons.
Electron gain enthalpy: Cl more negative than F (and S than O) due to crowding; noble gases positive.
Electronegativity rises across a period, falls down a group; oxides go basic → amphoteric → acidic.
Second-period elements are anomalous (small size, no d orbitals); diagonal pairs: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.

visual.alt: Summary table of three trends across a period and down a group

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Size falls across a period and rises down a group. Ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity do the opposite. The exceptions, like boron and oxygen, come from subshell structure. Electron gain enthalpy is most negative for chlorine, not fluorine. First elements of groups behave anomalously, and diagonal neighbours resemble each other.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: For any trend, give the cause: nuclear charge, shells added, or shielding.
For Be/B and N/O, quote subshell structure, not just “stability”.
For isoelectronic ions, state the electron count, then compare nuclear charge.
When explaining Cl > F, mention the small, crowded 2p subshell of fluorine.
Give a pair and two shared properties for a diagonal relationship.

rows: Ionisation enthalpy of O is higher than N
N has the half-filled 2p³; N > O
Fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy
Anions are smaller than their atoms

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Always state the reason behind a trend, whether it is nuclear charge, extra shells, or shielding. Name the subshell structure behind anomalies in ionisation enthalpy. Count electrons before comparing isoelectronic ions. For chlorine versus fluorine, mention the crowded second shell. And for diagonal relationships, name the pair and two properties they share.

notes.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties — Notes

sections.heading: 1. From triads to the modern periodic law
sections.body_md:
**Döbereiner (1817):** triads in which the middle atomic mass is close to the mean of the outer two (Li, Na, K: mean of 6.9 and 39.1 is 23.0, close to 23.0 for Na). **Newlands (1866):** law of octaves, every eighth element resembles the first; holds only up to calcium. **Mendeleev (1869):** properties are a periodic function of atomic mass; gaps were left for undiscovered elements (eka-boron, eka-aluminium, eka-silicon, later scandium, gallium, germanium); the order was sometimes reversed to keep similar elements together (Te, I). Limitations: position of hydrogen, isotopes, some pairs in the wrong mass order.

**Moseley (1913)** found that X-ray frequencies depend on nuclear charge, so the **modern periodic law** states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic numbers**. This puts Ar before K, Co before Ni and Te before I.

key_terms.definition_md: Three elements of similar properties, the middle mass being the mean of the outer two.
Newlands’ observation that every eighth element repeats properties.
Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

visual.alt: Four stages of classification

sections.heading: 2. The long form of the table and names for Z > 100
sections.body_md:
The long form has **18 groups** and **7 periods**. Period lengths come from the subshells that fill: 2 (1s), 8 (2s 2p), 8 (3s 3p), 18 (4s 3d 4p), 18 (5s 4d 5p), 32 (6s 4f 5d 6p), 32 (7s 5f 6d 7p); total 118.

**IUPAC temporary names:** roots nil (0), un (1), bi (2), tri (3), quad (4), pent (5), hex (6), sept (7), oct (8), enn (9) are joined in the order of the digits and followed by **-ium**; the symbol takes the first letter of each root. Examples: ununennium (Uue) for Z = 119, unbinilium (Ubn) for Z = 120, unbitrium (Ubt) for Z = 123.

key_terms.definition_md: IUPAC name built from numerical roots for a new element until a permanent name is approved.
A horizontal row; its number is the outermost shell being filled.
A vertical column of the long-form table (1 to 18).

visual.alt: Numerical roots

sections.heading: 3. Blocks, period and group from the configuration
sections.body_md: The **block** is the subshell receiving the last electron: **s** (groups 1 and 2, and He), **p** (groups 13 to 18), **d** (groups 3 to 12) and **f** (lanthanoids and actinoids). **Period** = highest shell number occupied. **Group:** s-block = number of valence electrons; p-block = 12 + number of p electrons; d-block = (n − 1)d electrons + ns electrons. Examples: As (Z = 33) [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³, p-block, period 4, group 15; Cd (Z = 48) [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s², d-block, period 5, group 12; Ba (Z = 56) [Xe] 6s², s-block, period 6, group 2.

key_terms.definition_md: Elements whose last electron enters an s subshell.
Elements (groups 3–12) whose last electron enters a (n−1)d subshell; transition elements.
Lanthanoids and actinoids; last electron enters 4f or 5f.

sections.heading: 4. Metals, non-metals, metalloids and other categories
sections.body_md: About four-fifths of the elements are **metals** (lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors; basic or amphoteric oxides). **Non-metals** lie at the top right and form anions or share electrons. **Metalloids** (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) lie along the staircase line and show intermediate behaviour. **Representative** elements are s- and p-block elements except group 18; **transition** elements are d-block; **inner transition** elements are f-block; **noble gases** have complete outer shells (ns² np⁶, He 1s²).

key_terms.definition_md: An element with properties between those of metals and non-metals.
A group 18 element with a complete outer shell.

sections.heading: 5. Atomic and ionic radii
sections.body_md: Radius falls across a period (rising nuclear charge, same shell) and rises down a group (new shells). Atomic radii (pm; metallic for metals, covalent for non-metals): Li 152, Be 111, B 88, C 77, N 74, O 66, F 64; Na 186, Mg 160, Al 143, Si 117, P 110, S 104, Cl 99. Van der Waals radius > covalent radius. A cation is smaller than its atom and an anion larger (Na 186 → Na⁺ 102; Cl 99 → Cl⁻ 181). **Isoelectronic** species: the radius falls as nuclear charge rises, N³⁻ 171 > O²⁻ 140 > F⁻ 133 > Na⁺ 102 > Mg²⁺ 72 > Al³⁺ 54 pm.

key_terms.definition_md: Half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element.
Having the same number of electrons.

sections.heading: 6. Ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity
sections.body_md:
**Ionisation enthalpy** rises across a period and falls down a group; it increases with nuclear charge and falls with size and screening (penetration s > p > d > f). Exceptions: Be (899) > B (801) because 2s penetrates more than 2p; N (1402) > O (1314) because N has half-filled 2p³ and O has a paired electron; likewise Mg > Al and P > S. Successive values jump after the valence electrons are removed.

**Electron gain enthalpy** is most negative for halogens; Cl (-349) is more negative than F (-328) because F is so small that its 2p subshell is crowded; noble gases have positive values; the second electron gain is always positive. **Electronegativity** (Pauling) rises across a period and falls down a group; F = 4.0, O = 3.5, N = 3.0, Cl = 3.0.

key_terms.definition_md: Enthalpy change for removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
Enthalpy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron; negative if energy is released.
Tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons.

sections.heading: 7. Valency, chemical character, anomalous behaviour and diagonal relationships
sections.body_md:
**Valency** is read from hydride or oxide formulae: period 3 hydrides NaH, MgH₂, AlH₃, SiH₄, PH₃, H₂S, HCl show 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1. Oxides go **basic** (Na₂O, MgO), **amphoteric** (Al₂O₃) and **acidic** (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇) across period 3. Amphoteric: $\ce{Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O}$ and $\ce{Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O -> 2NaAl(OH)4}$.

**Second-period anomalies:** small size, high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy, no d orbitals, so maximum covalence 4 (NCl₃ but PCl₅), and pπ–pπ multiple bonds. **Diagonal relationships:** Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si, owing to similar charge-to-size ratio and electronegativity (Be and Al both 1.5).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing “atomic mass” in the modern periodic law (it is atomic number).
- Forgetting that helium is s-block but placed in group 18.
- Saying fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy (chlorine does).
- Explaining the N/O ionisation anomaly without mentioning half-filled 2p³ and electron pairing in O.
- Comparing isoelectronic ions by atomic number of the neutral atom instead of nuclear charge of the ion.
- Writing names for Z > 100 digit by digit but leaving off the ending “ium”.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, a trend or a name.
- 2-mark reasoning: the fact and its cause (nuclear charge, shells, shielding, subshell structure).
- Data items: read the jump, compare values, then give the conclusion.

cards.front_md: What was Döbereiner’s triad rule?
cards.back_md: The mass of the middle element is about the mean of the other two (Li, Na, K).

cards.front_md: What did Newlands’ law of octaves state?
cards.back_md: Every eighth element resembles the first when elements are arranged by atomic mass; it held only up to calcium.

cards.front_md: Mendeleev’s periodic law?
cards.back_md: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.

cards.front_md: Which three elements did Mendeleev predict, and what were they later called?
cards.back_md: Eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon, found as scandium, gallium and germanium.

cards.front_md: Modern periodic law?
cards.back_md: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers (Moseley).

cards.front_md: Name two pairs placed against the order of atomic mass by Mendeleev.
cards.back_md: Te before I, and Co before Ni (also Ar before K).

cards.front_md: How many elements are in periods 1 to 7?
Why does the sixth period have 32 elements?
cards.back_md: The subshells 6s, 4f, 5d and 6p fill: 2 + 14 + 10 + 6.

cards.front_md: Root for each digit 0 to 9 in IUPAC names?
cards.back_md: nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn.

cards.front_md: Name and symbol for Z = 119?
cards.back_md: Ununennium, Uue.

cards.front_md: How is the block of an element decided?
cards.back_md: By the subshell into which the last electron enters.

cards.front_md: Group number rule for p-block elements?
cards.back_md: 12 + number of p electrons in the valence shell.

cards.front_md: Group number rule for d-block elements?
cards.back_md: (n − 1)d electrons + ns electrons, giving groups 3 to 12.

cards.front_md: Period number from configuration?
cards.back_md: The principal quantum number of the outermost occupied shell.

cards.front_md: Which s-block element is placed in group 18?
cards.back_md: Helium, 1s².

cards.front_md: Which elements are metalloids?
cards.back_md: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.

cards.front_md: What are inner transition elements?
cards.back_md: The f-block: lanthanoids (4f) and actinoids (5f).

cards.front_md: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period?
cards.back_md: Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell.

cards.front_md: Why is a cation smaller than its atom?
cards.back_md: Electrons are lost (often a whole shell) while the nuclear charge stays the same, so the rest are pulled in.

cards.front_md: Which is larger, Cl or Cl⁻?
cards.back_md: Cl⁻ (181 pm against 99 pm): extra electron repulsion.

cards.front_md: Order of radii: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻?
cards.back_md: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻ (isoelectronic; higher nuclear charge is smaller).

cards.front_md: Define ionisation enthalpy.
cards.back_md: Energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

cards.front_md: Order of penetration of orbitals of one shell?
cards.back_md: s > p > d > f.

cards.front_md: Why is Be higher than B in ionisation enthalpy?
cards.back_md: The 2s electron of Be penetrates more than the 2p electron of B.

cards.front_md: Why is N higher than O in ionisation enthalpy?
cards.back_md: N has the stable half-filled 2p³; O has a paired 2p electron that is easier to remove.

cards.front_md: What does a large jump in successive ionisation enthalpies show?
cards.back_md: That the valence electrons are all removed and the next comes from an inner shell.

cards.front_md: Why is Cl more negative than F in electron gain enthalpy?
cards.back_md: The very small 2p subshell of F repels the incoming electron more.

cards.front_md: Electronegativity trend?
cards.back_md: Increases across a period, decreases down a group; F = 4.0 is highest.

cards.front_md: How do oxides change across period 3?
cards.back_md: Basic (Na₂O, MgO), amphoteric (Al₂O₃), then acidic (SiO₂ to Cl₂O₇).

cards.front_md: Why is the covalence of nitrogen limited to 4?
cards.back_md: There are no d orbitals in the second shell.

cards.front_md: Name three diagonal pairs.
cards.back_md: Li–Mg, Be–Al and B–Si.

questions.stem_md: Mendeleev placed iodine (relative atomic mass 126.9) after tellurium (127.6) in his table. The modern periodic law supports this placement because:

options.text_md: iodine has a smaller number of isotopes than tellurium
iodine and tellurium have the same number of valence electrons
tellurium forms no compounds with hydrogen
the atomic number of iodine (53) is one more than that of tellurium (52)

questions.solution_md: The modern law orders elements by atomic number, not mass. Iodine has the larger atomic number, so it comes second even though it is lighter — option (d). Valence electrons differ (7 and 6), so (b) is false.

questions.stem_md: Mendeleev left a gap under silicon in his table and predicted an element of atomic mass near 72 with an oxide of formula $\ce{XO2}$. The element later discovered to fill this gap was:
questions.solution_md: The gap under silicon was called eka-silicon; germanium (mass 72.6, oxide GeO₂) matched it — option (d). Gallium (a) filled the gap under aluminium and scandium (b) the one under boron.

questions.stem_md: Before a permanent name was approved, the element with atomic number 112 had the systematic name ununbium. Its three-letter symbol was:
questions.solution_md: Use the first letter of each root: un (1), un (1), bi (2) give Uub, with a capital first letter only — option (a). Uun is the symbol that was used for element 110 (d).

questions.stem_md: The first period in which a subshell with l = 3 begins to fill, and the number of elements in that period, are:
questions.solution_md: An f subshell (l = 3) first fills as 4f, which comes in the sixth period after 6s. That period fills 6s, 4f, 5d and 6p: 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32 elements — option (b). The seventh period (d) is the second with f elements.

questions.stem_md: A laboratory reports a new element of atomic number 127. Its systematic name and symbol are:
questions.solution_md: The digits 1, 2, 7 give the roots un, bi and sept, so the name is unbiseptium and the symbol Ubs — option (c). The others use the wrong digit (a, d) or the digits in the wrong order (b).

questions.stem_md: Match each digit used in a systematic element name with its IUPAC numerical root.
questions.solution_md: The roots are 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct and 9 enn.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Newlands’ law of octaves could be applied equally well to all the elements known in his time, including those heavier than calcium.
questions.solution_md: False. The pattern held only up to calcium; beyond it, elements placed in the same column no longer resembled each other.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Atomic number, rather than atomic mass, is the better basis for classifying elements.

**Reason (R):** Isotopes of an element differ in mass but have the same atomic number and the same chemical properties.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Since isotopes of one element have different masses yet identical chemistry, mass cannot decide an element’s place, while the atomic number can; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the IUPAC systematic name of an element, the digit 4 is written with the numerical root ___.
questions.solution_md: The root for 4 is **quad**, as in unquadnilium (Z = 140).

questions.stem_md: Phosphorus (31), arsenic and antimony (121.8) are placed together as a Döbereiner triad. Using the triad rule, what atomic mass would be predicted for arsenic?
questions.solution_md: The middle mass is the mean of the other two: $\dfrac{31 + 121.8}{2} = 76.4$. (The measured mass of arsenic is 74.9, so the rule is only approximate.)

marking_scheme.step: Mean of the outer two masses, 76.4

questions.stem_md: An element is reported with the systematic name unbiennium. What is its atomic number?
questions.solution_md: un = 1, bi = 2, enn = 9, so the digits are 1, 2, 9 and $Z = 129$.

questions.stem_md: State the modern periodic law. How does it overcome the difficulty Mendeleev met with the order of cobalt and nickel?

answer.model_answer_md: The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. Cobalt is heavier than nickel (58.9 against 58.7), so a mass-based table would put nickel first, against their chemistry. By atomic number, cobalt (27) comes before nickel (28), so the anomaly disappears.

questions.solution_md: Law in terms of atomic number; apply it to Co and Ni.

marking_scheme.step: Co (27) before Ni (28), so no anomaly

questions.stem_md: Write the systematic IUPAC names and three-letter symbols of the elements with atomic numbers 115 and 130.

answer.model_answer_md: For Z = 115 the digits are 1, 1, 5, giving the roots un, un, pent: ununpentium, symbol Uup. For Z = 130 the digits 1, 3, 0 give un, tri, nil: untrinilium, symbol Utn. Each name ends in -ium and each symbol takes the first letter of each root.

questions.solution_md: Convert digit by digit and add -ium.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a Döbereiner triad? Show that lithium (6.9), sodium (23.0) and potassium (39.1) form one.

answer.model_answer_md: A triad is a set of three elements of similar properties in which the atomic mass of the middle element is about the mean of the other two. For lithium and potassium the mean is (6.9 + 39.1)/2 = 23.0, which equals the atomic mass of sodium, so the three form a triad.

questions.solution_md: Definition and a calculation of the mean of the outer two.

marking_scheme.step: Mean 23.0 equals the mass of sodium

questions.stem_md: State two achievements and two limitations of Mendeleev’s periodic table.

answer.model_answer_md: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted the properties of eka-aluminium and eka-silicon, which matched gallium and germanium when they were found; he also corrected some atomic masses by placing elements according to properties. Hydrogen had no proper position, since it resembles both alkali metals and halogens, and isotopes could not be accommodated. A few elements were in the wrong order of mass.

questions.solution_md: Predictions and gaps as achievements; hydrogen, isotopes and mass inversions as limitations.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Mendeleev’s periodic law and the modern periodic law.

(b) Explain why Mendeleev left gaps and how his predictions for eka-silicon were confirmed.

(c) Write the systematic name and symbol for the element with atomic number 121, and explain how the roots were chosen.

answer.model_answer_md: Mendeleev’s law says that properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses; the modern law replaces mass by atomic number. Mendeleev arranged elements so that those with similar properties fell in one group; where no known element fitted, he left a gap, for example under silicon, predicting an element of mass about 72 and a dioxide. Germanium, found later, had mass 72.6 and formed GeO₂, matching the prediction and winning acceptance for the table. For Z = 121 the digits 1, 2, 1 are written with the roots un, bi and un, and the ending -ium is added: unbiunium, symbol Ubu.

questions.solution_md: Both laws; gaps and a confirmed prediction; digit-by-digit roots.

questions.stem_md: An element has the valence-shell configuration 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³ (all inner shells complete). It is placed in the:
questions.solution_md: The last electron enters 5p, so it is a p-block element. The outer shell is the fifth, so period 5, and the group is 12 + 3 = 15 — option (d). The filled 4d subshell does not make it a d-block element (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following sets contains only metalloids?
questions.solution_md: Silicon, germanium and antimony all lie on the staircase line — option (a). Carbon (b) is a non-metal, tin and lead (c) are metals, and phosphorus (d) is a non-metal.

questions.stem_md: An element has the valence configuration 3d⁵ 4s². Its group number in the long-form periodic table is:
questions.solution_md: For d-block elements the group number is the sum of the (n − 1)d and ns electrons: 5 + 2 = 7 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The last electron of an element enters a 4f orbital. The element belongs to:

options.text_md: the lanthanoids, in the sixth period
the actinoids, in the seventh period
the transition elements of the fourth period

questions.solution_md: The 4f subshell fills in the sixth period, so the element is a lanthanoid, an inner transition element — option (a). Actinoids (b) fill 5f.

questions.stem_md: Helium (1s²) is an s-block element but is placed in group 18 with the noble gases, because:

options.text_md: it has two electrons, as the group 2 metals do
it has two electrons in the p subshell
its outermost shell is complete, so it is chemically inert like the noble gases
it is a metal that is unreactive

questions.solution_md: A full outer shell gives stability and inertness, which is the property that defines group 18 — option (c). Group 2 metals (a) are reactive.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Helium is classified as an s-block element.

**Reason (R):** Helium is placed with the noble gases in group 18.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Helium is s-block because its last electron enters 1s; its position in group 18 is a different fact based on its complete shell, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The group number of a p-block element with the valence configuration ns² np⁵ is ___.
questions.solution_md: For p-block elements, group = 12 + number of p electrons = 12 + 5 = **17** (halogens).

questions.stem_md: What is the atomic number of the element in period 5 and group 14 of the long-form periodic table?
questions.solution_md: The noble gas before period 5 is krypton ($Z = 36$). Group 14 is the fourteenth column, so $Z = 36 + 14 = 50$ (tin).

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configuration of the element with atomic number 26 and state its block, period and group.

answer.model_answer_md: Z = 26 has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². The last electron enters 3d, so it is a d-block element; the outermost shell is the fourth, so period 4; the group is 6 + 2 = 8.

questions.solution_md: Write the configuration, then apply the rules for d-block.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain how the block, period and group of an element are found from its electronic configuration.

(b) Locate the elements with Z = 33 and Z = 48 in the periodic table.

(c) Why is the sixth period longer than the fourth period?

answer.model_answer_md: The block is given by the subshell receiving the last electron (s, p, d or f). The period is the principal quantum number of the outermost shell. The group is the number of valence electrons for s-block, 12 plus the p electrons for p-block, and the sum of (n − 1)d and ns electrons for d-block. Z = 33 is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³, a p-block element in period 4 and group 15. Z = 48 is [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s², a d-block element in period 5 and group 12. The sixth period fills 6s, 4f, 5d and 6p, which hold 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32 electrons, while the fourth fills only 4s, 3d and 4p, holding 18.

questions.solution_md: Rules for block, period and group; two locations; subshell capacities of periods 4 and 6.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
Three elements are described by their valence-shell configurations (inner shells complete).

| Element | Valence configuration |
|---|---|
| X | 3s² 3p⁴ |
| Y | 3d⁷ 4s² |
| Z | 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s² |

(Elements X, Y and Z are labels only, not symbols.)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) d-block

**(b)** Period 3 (outermost shell n = 3) and group 16 (12 + 4).

**(c)** (i) Y has 7 + 2 = 9 electrons beyond its core in 3d and 4s, so it is in group 9. Z has its 4f subshell, two shells inside the outermost, partly filled (4f⁷), so it is an f-block or inner transition element, a lanthanoid.

**OR** (ii) In X, the outer 3p subshell is filling, so it belongs to the p-block and is a representative element. In Y, the inner 3d subshell is being filled, so it is a d-block or transition element, with properties such as variable oxidation states.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The last electron of Y enters 3d, so Y is a d-block element — option (a). Its 4s electrons are in the outer shell, but the d subshell is the one filling.

**(b)** Outer shell 3; four p electrons give 12 + 4.

**(c)** (i) d + s electrons for the group; 4f filling for Z.

(ii) Representative: outer shell filling; transition: inner d subshell filling.

children.stem_md: To which block does Y belong?
children.solution_md: The last electron of Y enters 3d, so Y is a d-block element — option (a). Its 4s electrons are in the outer shell, but the d subshell is the one filling.

children.stem_md: Give the period and group of X.

answer.model_answer_md: Period 3 (outermost shell n = 3) and group 16 (12 + 4).

children.solution_md: Outer shell 3; four p electrons give 12 + 4.

answer.model_answer_md: Y has 7 + 2 = 9 electrons beyond its core in 3d and 4s, so it is in group 9. Z has its 4f subshell, two shells inside the outermost, partly filled (4f⁷), so it is an f-block or inner transition element, a lanthanoid.

children.solution_md: d + s electrons for the group; 4f filling for Z.

marking_scheme.step: Z: f subshell filling, inner transition

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain why X is a representative element but Y is not.

answer.model_answer_md: In X, the outer 3p subshell is filling, so it belongs to the p-block and is a representative element. In Y, the inner 3d subshell is being filled, so it is a d-block or transition element, with properties such as variable oxidation states.

alternatives.solution_md: Representative: outer shell filling; transition: inner d subshell filling.

marking_scheme.step: Y: inner d subshell filling, transition

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: In 2010 a team reported making a new element with atomic number 117. Until the name was approved, it was written with the systematic IUPAC name ununseptium and the symbol Uus. The roots used were un (1) and sept (7).

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** 118

**OR** (ii) A newly made element may exist for only a fraction of a second and needs confirmation, so it cannot yet receive a permanent name. **(b)** un = 1, un = 1, oct = 8, so $Z = 118$.

**(c)** (i) Last electron in 7p; period length from subshell capacities.

(ii) Permanent names wait for confirmation; the name is built mechanically.

children.stem_md: Which digit sequence produces the name in the passage?
children.solution_md: The name ununseptium is un, un, sept, which is the digits 1, 1, 7 in that order — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
Mendeleev described an undiscovered element, which he called eka-silicon, from the gap below silicon in his table. The table compares his predictions with the properties of germanium, found in 1886.

| Property | Predicted for eka-silicon | Observed for germanium |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic mass | 72 | 72.6 |
| Density / g cm⁻³ | 5.5 | 5.3 |
| Formula of oxide | $\ce{XO2}$ | $\ce{GeO2}$ |
| Formula of chloride | $\ce{XCl4}$ | $\ce{GeCl4}$ |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) The close match of predicted and observed values supported the periodic law.

**(b)** 0.83 %

**(c)** (i) Mendeleev had predicted the mass, density and compounds of eka-silicon before it was known. When germanium was found, its properties agreed closely with his predictions. This showed that the table captured a real pattern in the elements, not just a convenient list.

**OR** (ii) The last electron enters the 4p subshell, so germanium is a p-block element. The outermost shell is the fourth, giving period 4, and 12 + 2 = 14 gives its group. Four valence electrons explain the formulae GeO₂ and GeCl₄.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Every property is close to the prediction and the formulae agree exactly, which strongly supported the idea of periodicity — option (a). Formulae XO₂ and XCl₄ are those of a group 14 element (d).

**(b)** Excess as a percentage of the predicted value: $\dfrac{72.6 - 72}{72} \times 100 = 0.83$, so about 0.83 per cent.

**(c)** (i) A successful prediction is strong evidence for the law.

(ii) Last electron in 4p; outer shell 4; 12 + 2.

children.stem_md: Which statement about the data is correct?

options.text_md: The close match of predicted and observed values supported the periodic law.
The values differ so much that the prediction failed.
Only the atomic mass was predicted correctly.
The oxide and chloride formulae show that germanium is not in group 14.

children.solution_md: Every property is close to the prediction and the formulae agree exactly, which strongly supported the idea of periodicity — option (a). Formulae XO₂ and XCl₄ are those of a group 14 element (d).

children.stem_md: Calculate the percentage by which the observed atomic mass of germanium exceeds the predicted value (take 72.6 and 72; give the answer to two decimal places).
children.solution_md: Excess as a percentage of the predicted value: $\dfrac{72.6 - 72}{72} \times 100 = 0.83$, so about 0.83 per cent.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Why did the discovery of germanium persuade chemists to accept Mendeleev’s table?

answer.model_answer_md: Mendeleev had predicted the mass, density and compounds of eka-silicon before it was known. When germanium was found, its properties agreed closely with his predictions. This showed that the table captured a real pattern in the elements, not just a convenient list.

children.solution_md: A successful prediction is strong evidence for the law.

marking_scheme.step: Showed the table reflects a real periodic pattern

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The modern table places germanium in group 14, period 4. Explain this position using its configuration, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p².

answer.model_answer_md: The last electron enters the 4p subshell, so germanium is a p-block element. The outermost shell is the fourth, giving period 4, and 12 + 2 = 14 gives its group. Four valence electrons explain the formulae GeO₂ and GeCl₄.

marking_scheme.step: p-block, period 4 from the outer shell

questions.stem_md: The species Br⁻, Se²⁻, Rb⁺ and Sr²⁺ all have 36 electrons. Which has the smallest radius?
questions.solution_md: For isoelectronic species the one with the greatest nuclear charge pulls the electrons in most. Sr²⁺ (Z = 38) is highest, so it is the smallest — option (a). Se²⁻ (Z = 34) is the largest.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpy of phosphorus (1012 kJ mol⁻¹) is greater than that of sulfur (999 kJ mol⁻¹), although sulfur has the higher nuclear charge. The best explanation is:

options.text_md: phosphorus atoms are smaller than sulfur atoms
sulfur has no electron in its 3s orbital
phosphorus has fewer inner shells than sulfur
phosphorus has a half-filled 3p subshell, while one 3p electron of sulfur is paired and easier to remove

questions.solution_md: The half-filled p³ arrangement of phosphorus is stable, and the paired electron in sulfur is repelled by its partner, so it leaves more easily — option (d). In fact sulfur is the smaller atom (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these properties is shared by beryllium and aluminium, an example of a diagonal relationship?

options.text_md: They have the same number of valence electrons.
Both burn in nitrogen to form peroxides.

questions.solution_md: BeO and Al₂O₃ both react with acids and bases — option (d). Beryllium has two valence electrons and aluminium three (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about atomic radii is correct?

options.text_md: The covalent radius of chlorine is greater than that of sulfur.
The van der Waals radius of an atom is greater than its covalent radius.
Atomic radius increases from lithium to fluorine across the second period.
A neutral atom is smaller than its cation.

questions.solution_md: Non-bonded atoms touch at a larger distance than bonded atoms, so the van der Waals radius is greater — option (b). Across the period radii fall (c), and a cation is smaller than its atom (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of Cr²⁺, Cr³⁺ and Cr⁶⁺ has the largest radius, and why?

options.text_md: Cr⁶⁺, because it has lost the most electrons
Cr³⁺, because it lies in the middle
Cr²⁺, because it has the most electrons held by the same nucleus
All three are equal, as the nucleus is the same

questions.solution_md: The nuclear charge is fixed, so the ion with the most electrons is the least tightly held and so the largest: Cr²⁺ > Cr³⁺ > Cr⁶⁺ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpies of N, O and F, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 1402, 1314 and 1681 in some order. Which assignment is correct?
questions.solution_md: Fluorine has the highest value (smallest atom, highest nuclear charge). Nitrogen exceeds oxygen because of its half-filled 2p³ subshell, so the order is O < N < F — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An element has successive ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of 899, 1757, 14849 and 21007. It is most likely in group:
questions.solution_md: The huge rise from the second to the third value (about 8.5 times) shows that the third electron comes from an inner shell, so two valence electrons are present: group 2 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of O, S, F and Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
questions.solution_md: Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more negative than F (−328), whose small 2p subshell is crowded — option (a). S and O release less energy because they need two electrons to complete the octet.

questions.stem_md: Pauling electronegativities are H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5 and F 4.0. Which bond is the most polar?
questions.solution_md: The polarity increases with the electronegativity difference: H–C 0.4, H–N 0.9, H–O 1.4, H–F 1.9. The largest is H–F — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The oxide of a third-period element dissolves in both dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide. The element is:
questions.solution_md: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases is amphoteric. In the third period only Al₂O₃ is amphoteric — option (b). Na₂O is basic (a); SiO₂ and SO₃ are acidic.

questions.stem_md: An element lies in period 3 and group 15. The formula of its hydride is:
questions.solution_md: Z = 15 (phosphorus) needs three hydrogens to complete its octet: PH₃ — option (c). NH₃ (d) is the hydride of the period 2 member of the group.

questions.stem_md: Nitrogen forms NCl₃ but not NCl₅, whereas phosphorus forms both PCl₃ and PCl₅. The reason is that nitrogen:

options.text_md: is more electronegative than phosphorus and forms ionic bonds
has a half-filled 2p subshell that cannot be disturbed
has no d orbitals in its second shell, so it cannot exceed a covalence of four
is a gas while phosphorus is a solid

questions.solution_md: Phosphorus can use vacant 3d orbitals to expand its valence shell, but the second shell has only 2s and 2p, so nitrogen’s maximum covalence is four — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An anion is larger than the atom from which it is formed.

**Reason (R):** The nuclear charge of an anion is lower than that of its parent atom.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the nuclear charge does not change when an electron is added. The anion is larger because the same positive charge now attracts more electrons, and the electrons repel one another more — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.

**Reason (R):** Chlorine is more electronegative than fluorine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true because the 2p subshell of the small fluorine atom is crowded. R is false, since fluorine (4.0) is more electronegative than chlorine (3.0) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Boron has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than beryllium.

**Reason (R):** The 2p electron of boron is less penetrating than the 2s electron of beryllium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: beryllium (899 kJ mol⁻¹) exceeds boron (801). R is true, and it is the reason for beryllium’s higher value — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The first ionisation enthalpy decreases from lithium to caesium.

**Reason (R):** Down the group the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The larger distance and increased shielding outweigh the greater nuclear charge, so the electron is removed more easily; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A cation is always larger than the atom from which it is formed.
questions.solution_md: False. A cation is smaller: electrons are removed (often a whole outer shell), while the nuclear charge is unchanged and holds the rest more tightly.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen (O⁻ gaining an electron to form O²⁻) is negative.
questions.solution_md: False. The incoming electron is repelled by the negative ion, so energy must be supplied: the second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is positive.

questions.stem_md: Species that have the same number of electrons, such as Na⁺ and F⁻, are called ___.
questions.solution_md: Species with equal numbers of electrons are **isoelectronic**.

questions.stem_md: Match each oxide with its nature.
questions.solution_md: Sodium oxide is basic, aluminium oxide is amphoteric, sulfur trioxide is acidic and carbon monoxide is neutral.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpy of sodium is 496 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy, in kJ, is needed to convert 0.25 mol of gaseous sodium atoms into gaseous Na⁺ ions?
questions.solution_md: Energy $= 0.25 \times 496 = 124$, so $124\ \text{kJ}$.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpy of sodium is 496 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy needed to remove an electron from a single sodium atom, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J. (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: Energy per atom, in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$: $\dfrac{496000 \times 10^{19}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 8.24$, so the energy is $8.24 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ per atom.

questions.stem_md: The first and second ionisation enthalpies of magnesium are 737 and 1451 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert one mole of gaseous Mg atoms into gaseous Mg²⁺ ions.
questions.solution_md: Both electrons must be removed, one after the other: $737 + 1451 = 2188$, so $2188\ \text{kJ}$.

marking_scheme.step: Sum of the first two enthalpies, 2188 kJ

questions.stem_md: The Br–Br bond length in a bromine molecule is 228 pm. What is the covalent radius of bromine, in pm?
questions.solution_md: The covalent radius is half the bond length: $\dfrac{228}{2} = 114$, so $114\ \text{pm}$.

questions.stem_md: An element has the successive ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): 1012, 1907, 2914, 4964, 6274 and 21267. How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.solution_md: Ratios of successive values: 1.88, 1.53, 1.70, 1.26, 3.39. The largest jump follows the fifth removal, so the number of valence electrons is $5$.

marking_scheme.step: Largest jump after the 5th: 5 valence electrons

questions.stem_md: Explain why (a) the sodium ion is smaller than the sodium atom, and (b) the fluoride ion is larger than the fluorine atom.

answer.model_answer_md: Sodium loses its single 3s electron, so the ion has one shell fewer, and ten electrons are held by the unchanged nuclear charge of eleven. Fluorine gains an electron, so nine protons now hold ten electrons, and the extra electron-electron repulsion makes the electron cloud expand.

questions.solution_md: Cation: loss of a shell and the same nuclear charge; anion: extra repulsion.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Cation smaller: shell lost, nucleus holds fewer electrons
(b) Anion larger: more electron repulsion, same nuclear charge

questions.stem_md: Why do noble gases have large positive electron gain enthalpies, and why is the second electron gain enthalpy of an element always positive?

answer.model_answer_md: A noble gas atom has a complete shell, so an extra electron must enter a new, higher shell and be shielded, which requires energy. When a second electron is added to a negative ion, the electron is repelled by the existing charge, so energy must again be supplied; the second value is therefore positive.

questions.solution_md: New shell for noble gases; repulsion by the anion for the second gain.

marking_scheme.step: Second gain: repulsion by the negative ion

questions.stem_md: What is a diagonal relationship? Name the pair of elements that shows it with lithium and give two shared properties.

answer.model_answer_md: A diagonal relationship is the resemblance between an element and the one diagonally below and to its right, owing to a similar charge-to-size ratio. Lithium resembles magnesium: both form a nitride directly with nitrogen, and the carbonates of both decompose on heating to give the oxide.

answer.model_answer_md: The oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇), because the elements change from metallic to non-metallic across the period, so the oxides of metals give bases with water and those of non-metals give acids. questions.stem_md:
(a) Define first ionisation enthalpy and name the factors that affect it.

(b) Explain the general trend across the second period from Li to Ne.

(c) Explain why the values for boron and oxygen are lower than expected from this trend.

answer.model_answer_md: First ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It rises with nuclear charge and with penetration of the electron, and falls with larger size and more shielding. Across the second period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so atoms shrink and the energy rises from lithium to neon. Boron is lower than beryllium because its 2p electron is less penetrating than the 2s electron of beryllium. Oxygen is lower than nitrogen because nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p subshell, while in oxygen one 2p electron is paired and repelled by its partner, so it is removed more easily.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity, and state one difference between them.

(b) Explain why chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, although fluorine is more electronegative.

(c) State the trend in electronegativity across a period and down a group, with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron; electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared electron pair. The first belongs to an isolated atom and is measured in kJ mol⁻¹, while the second is a relative number for a bonded atom. Fluorine is so small that its 2p subshell is crowded, so an incoming electron meets strong repulsion and less energy is released; chlorine’s larger 3p subshell has more room. Electronegativity rises across a period because the nuclear charge increases and the atom shrinks, and falls down a group because the atoms grow and the shared pair is farther from the nucleus.

questions.solution_md: Two definitions and a difference; crowding in fluorine; trends with causes.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why do the elements of the second period show anomalous behaviour compared with other members of their groups?

(b) Illustrate with the chlorides of nitrogen and phosphorus.

(c) Explain the diagonal relationship between beryllium and aluminium, giving two similarities.

answer.model_answer_md: Second-period elements are very small and have high electronegativity and ionisation enthalpy, and they have no d orbitals in the valence shell, so their covalence cannot exceed four. Nitrogen forms only NCl₃, whereas phosphorus, with vacant 3d orbitals, forms both PCl₃ and PCl₅. Beryllium and aluminium resemble each other because the higher charge of aluminium is offset by its larger size, giving a similar charge-to-size ratio and equal electronegativity (1.5). Both oxides are amphoteric, and both form chlorides that are largely covalent.
